99.title: Seva of the hands
99.hook: washing dishes, sweeping, cooking: the body's seva
99.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, Sikhs and visitors volunteer to cook, clean, sweep and wash the langar dishes, often reciting or listening to gurbani as they work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the joda ghar, and the honored seva of minding shoes. Your line was start at the shoes. Did you do a job that felt beneath you, first and well? Day ninety-nine.
screen: `START WITH THE SHOES — START AT THE SHOES.`

segments.voice: The back of a big gurdwara kitchen, after langar. A mountain of steel plates, the kind with little sections for dal and rice and sweet. A line of people stands along a trough of hot, soapy water. One scrapes. One scrubs. One rinses. One dries and stacks. Their sleeves are soaked. Nobody is in charge of anyone. A teenager is next to a man who runs a company, and they've fallen into the same rhythm, plate after plate after plate. It looks like the chore you get through before the spiritual part. Sikhs would say this is the spiritual part.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN OF STEEL PLATES.` → `SCRAPE, SCRUB, RINSE, STACK.` → `THIS IS THE SPIRITUAL PART.`

segments.voice: Sikhs often talk about seva in three ways: tan, man and dhan. Body, mind and wealth. Today is tan, the seva of the body: washing, sweeping, cooking, carrying, fixing. Tomorrow, the purse. After that, the mind. Why does the body's seva matter so much? Kind thoughts are easy. Scrubbing someone else's pot is harder, and pride feels it. When your hands do the humble work, the teaching goes all the way in. You met the model for this on day forty-nine. Before he became the third Guru, Amar Das was an old man who carried water for Guru Angad, before dawn, from the river, for years. Tradition says he never let the work stop, even in the dark and the rain. The Guru he became was shaped by those buckets. The Guru Granth Sahib has a couplet among the saloks of Kabir where Namdev tells Trilochan, in paraphrase: do all your work with hands and feet, and keep your mind with the Pure One. Punjabis put it shorter: hands at work, heart with the beloved. You don't have to choose between doing and remembering. While the hands wash, the mind can say Waheguru. While the broom moves, the heart can be still. The chore becomes a kind of prayer. And there's one more thing hands teach. Doing the work together makes a sangat. You can argue with someone in a meeting. It's much harder to stay angry with a person when you've stood side by side for an hour, passing them wet plates. So in Sikh life the hands are not the servants of the spirit. They're one of the ways the spirit gets anywhere at all.
screen: `TAN, MAN, DHAN: BODY, MIND, WEALTH.` · `KIND THOUGHTS ARE EASY; POTS AREN'T.` · `AMAR DAS AND THE WATER.` · `HANDS AT WORK, HEART WITH THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `HANDS CAN PRAY.`

segments.voice: Take one dish, a cup or a plate, even a spoon, and wash it slowly. Feel the water's temperature. Watch the soap slide. Turn it in your hands. If you can't get to a sink, pick up any object near you and wipe it clean with the same care. With each movement, let a word ride along: Waheguru, if you like, or just thank you. Hands at work, heart somewhere quiet. The bell holds the time.
Seva of the hands. Tan seva, the body's service: washing, sweeping, cooking, carrying, done with the heart somewhere else, somewhere good.
Your line: hands can pray. Today, pick one chore you usually rush, and do it slowly, with a word riding along. Day ninety-nine.

100.title: Seva of the purse
100.hook: many Sikhs set aside a tenth of what they earn for the common good
100.howItsDone: Many Sikhs set aside daswandh, a tenth of their earnings, for the gurdwara, the langar, education and relief work; others give their time in its place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seva of the hands: dishes, brooms, buckets. Your line was hands can pray. Did a chore go slowly, with a word riding along? And by the way: day one hundred.
screen: `SEVA OF THE HANDS — HANDS CAN PRAY.`

segments.voice: A hundred days. Take a second with that. Now think about payday. The money lands, and within an hour most of it already has somewhere to be. Rent. The phone bill. Groceries. That thing you've been waiting to buy. By the time you think about giving any away, it's whatever's left, which usually isn't much. Now imagine doing it the other way around. The money lands, and before the rent, before anything, one small slice is set aside. Not for you. Not for your family. For whoever needs it. Many Sikhs have a word for that slice, and it's older than any bank.
screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED.` → `PAYDAY, AND IT'S ALL SPOKEN FOR.` → `ONE SLICE, SET ASIDE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Daswandh. Das is ten. Vandh is a share, a portion. A tenth share. It's the seva of the purse, dhan seva, the third of tan, man and dhan. Many Sikhs set aside a tenth of what they earn for the common good: the gurdwara, the langar, schools, disaster relief, a neighbor in trouble. Tradition says the practice took shape in the time of the fourth and fifth Gurus, when Sikhs were asked to give a tenth, and those gifts helped build the city of Amritsar and the Harmandir Sahib you met on day sixty. You first met the tenth on day ten, inside the second pillar, share what you earn. Today, the part of its story that day left out: who carried the money. Sikhs lived in towns and villages far from the Guru, so tradition says agents called masands were appointed to collect the offerings and bring them in. For a while it worked. Then, tradition says, some masands kept what they collected and lorded it over the people who gave. Guru Gobind Singh ended the masand system and asked Sikhs to bring their offerings to the Guru directly. So daswandh comes with two halves. Give honestly, and make sure what's given is handled honestly. Many Sikhs today still ask where their tenth goes: a gurdwara committee with open accounts, a langar, a school, a relief fund they trust. A tenth isn't a law you're fined for missing. Sikhs treat it as a discipline and an ideal. Some give more. People with very little give time instead. And many Sikhs say the money came from the Giver in the first place, so daswandh is just passing some of it on.
screen: `DAS AND VANDH: A TENTH SHARE.` · `BUILDING AMRITSAR, A TENTH AT A TIME.` · `THE MASANDS WHO CARRIED IT.` · `GIVEN HONESTLY, HANDLED HONESTLY.` · then, large: `A TENTH, FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of what comes in for you in a month or a week: a paycheck, an allowance, whatever it is. You don't need an exact number. Now find a tenth of it. Just do the math in your head. Hold that number for a moment. Notice how it feels: small, huge, scary, easy. There's no right answer. Then picture it going somewhere good, one real place or person. You're not committing to anything. Just looking. The bell holds the time.
Daswandh. A tenth share: the part of what you earn that many Sikhs set aside for others, first.
Your line: a tenth, for others. Today, work out your tenth, and give even a sliver of it somewhere, before you spend anything on yourself. Day one hundred.

101.title: Seva of the mind
101.hook: teaching, listening and sharing knowledge kindly are seva too
101.howItsDone: Sikh communities run weekend Gurmukhi and kirtan classes, tutoring and study circles, and many Sikhs count teaching and patient listening as seva alongside cooking and giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daswandh, the tenth share set aside first. Your line was a tenth, for others. Did you do the math, and give a sliver? Day one hundred one.

Somebody once taught you something small that stuck. A neighbor who showed you how to change a tire. A coworker who, in your first week, quietly explained how things really work around here. A grandparent who taught a recipe without measuring anything. No money changed hands. No dishes got washed. What they gave lives in your head now, and they may never have thought of it as a gift. Explaining something patiently, instead of sighing, is giving too. Sikhs have a name for that kind of giving, and it's the third of the three sevas.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SHOWED YOU HOW.` → `A GIFT THAT LIVES IN YOUR HEAD.` → `THE THIRD SEVA.`

segments.voice: Tan, dhan, and now man: the seva of the mind. Teaching what you know. Listening well. Sharing knowledge kindly, without making anyone feel small. You met a Guru who did this on day forty-five. Guru Angad took the Gurmukhi script and, tradition says, taught children to read it, so that ordinary people could read the Gurus' words for themselves. That was seva of the mind on a grand scale: knowledge handed out, not locked up. Guru Nanak says it in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: when learning is truly reflected on, it makes a person a benefactor of others. Knowledge that only makes you look clever hasn't finished its work. Knowledge that makes you useful has. There's a second half to this seva, and it's listening. In the Japji, Guru Nanak gives four whole stanzas to listening, suniai, and says that by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are erased. Listening is how you learn. But listening to another person, really listening, is also a gift you give. Someone who feels heard has been served. And one word in today's theme matters: kindly. Seva of the mind goes wrong when it turns into showing off, or correcting people so they feel stupid. The Sikh ideal is the opposite: humble, patient, glad to pass it on. Sikh communities do this in plain ways. Gurmukhi classes for children on weekends. Tutoring. Elders teaching the tunes of the hymns. Young people teaching elders how to use their phones. All of it counts. A mind can serve.
screen: `MAN — THE SEVA OF THE MIND.` · `ANGAD TEACHES CHILDREN TO READ.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · `LISTENING IS A GIFT TOO.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you know how to do that someone near you doesn't. A shortcut on the computer. How to fold a fitted sheet. A word in another language. A way to calm down before a hard call. Now think of who could use it. Picture yourself showing them, slowly, without hurry, without making them feel slow. Notice how it feels to be patient in your imagination. That's the rehearsal. The bell holds the time.
Seva of the mind. Man seva: teaching, listening, and sharing what you know, kindly, so that others are served.
Your line: give what you know. Today, teach someone one small thing, and then listen to one person all the way to the end. Day one hundred one.

screen: `DAY 101 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN SEVA FEEDS THE EGO.`

102.title: When seva feeds the ego
102.hook: serving to be seen feeds the very ego seva is meant to thin
102.howItsDone: Sikh teaching names haumai, ego, as the root obstacle between a person and God, and Sikhs are taught to do seva humbly and without seeking recognition so that it thins the ego rather than feeding it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seva of the mind: teaching and listening. Your line was give what you know. Did you teach someone one small thing? Day one hundred two.
screen: `SEVA OF THE MIND — GIVE WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Saturday morning, serving food at a shelter. Good work, and a tired, happy walk home. Then a tiny voice asks: should I post about it? Just one picture. Not to brag. Just so people know. Or it's quieter than that. All the dishes at a family dinner, washed, and a small wait for someone to notice. Nobody does, and it stings. That sting is worth paying attention to. It isn't the mark of a bad person. It's something the Gurus wrote about again and again, and today it gets a name.
screen: `SHOULD I POST ABOUT IT?` → `WAITING TO BE NOTICED.` → `THE STING HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Haumai. Hau means I. Mai means me. I, me. It's the word the Gurus use for ego: the self that puts itself at the center of everything, that wants credit, that keeps count. In Sikh teaching, haumai is the main thing that stands between a person and God. Not some outside enemy. The inside one. Here's the trap this week has been building toward. Seva is meant to thin haumai: you serve, you forget yourself, the I gets a little smaller. But if you serve in order to be seen, the seva itself becomes food for the ego. The more you do, the bigger it gets. Same dishes, same shoes, opposite result. That's why the Gurus keep stressing nishkam, without wanting. Now the hopeful part. Guru Angad has a line about it in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: haumai is a long, deep illness, but the medicine is within it too. The very place the sickness lives is where the cure can start. When you notice yourself wanting credit, that noticing is already the medicine working. Guru Nanak says in the Japji that someone who understands the divine order, the hukam, stops saying I. So the practice isn't to beat yourself up for wanting to be seen. That's just more I. The practice is to notice it, smile at it, and let it go, the way you'd smile at a child who wants you to watch them jump. Then do the next bit of service anyway. Serve, and then forget it.
screen: `HAU AND MAI: I, ME.` · `SEVA TO BE SEEN FEEDS THE I.` · `THE MEDICINE IS WITHIN IT TOO.` · `NOTICE IT, SMILE, LET IT GO.` · then, large: `SERVE, THEN FORGET IT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days of seva: the unseen kindness, the shoes, the dish, the tenth, the thing you taught. Did you want anyone to know? Find that moment. Don't judge it. Just see it clearly, like spotting a cat on a windowsill. Oh, there you are. Smile at it. Then let the breath carry it out. Do it again with any other moment that comes. The bell holds the time.
Haumai. I, me: the ego that wants credit, which seva is meant to thin, and which the Gurus say holds its own cure.
Your line: serve, then forget it. Today, when you catch yourself wanting credit, smile at it, and let it go. Day one hundred two.

103.title: Your weekly seva
103.hook: choose one small regular service you can actually keep
103.howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep a regular seva, such as a weekly shift in the gurdwara langar or cleaning, and families often serve together on the same day each week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai, the I that wants credit. Your line was serve, then forget it. Did you catch the wanting, and smile? Day one hundred three.

A big January resolution often goes like this. New shoes, big plans, five mornings a week, and by February the plan has quietly gone. Not from laziness. The plan was too big to keep. Meanwhile there's the neighbor who walks the same two blocks every evening, year after year, without any fuss. The small thing, kept, outlasts the big thing, dropped. Seva works the same way. This week brought an unseen kindness, the shoes, a dish, a tenth, a lesson taught. Today is the last day of seva week, and the question is simple: what will you actually keep?
screen: `THE JANUARY RESOLUTION.` → `TWO BLOCKS, EVERY EVENING.` → `WHAT WILL YOU ACTUALLY KEEP?`

segments.voice: In Sikh life, seva is less about big moments than about rhythm. Some Sikh families keep the same weekly seva for years. The same Sunday shift in the langar kitchen. The same job cleaning the gurdwara's floors before the week begins. Driving the same elderly neighbor to the same appointment. Nobody's counting. It's just what Sunday is. A gurdwara itself runs on this. Before anyone arrives, someone has already swept the floor, lit the stoves and set out the plates, and tomorrow someone will do it again. Nobody remembers a single morning. The mornings add up. That's what regular seva does. A single big act can feed haumai, the ego from yesterday: look what I did. A small act, repeated, gets boring to the ego, and that's the point. Around the hundredth time you wipe the same tables, there's nobody left to impress. There's only the table, and the people who'll eat there. So the advice is plain. Make it small. Make it specific. Make it regular. Not help more, but every Thursday I'll take my neighbor's bins out. Not give back, but the first Sunday of the month I'll cook at the gurdwara, or the food bank, or for the new parents down the hall. You can choose tan, man or dhan: your hands, your mind, your purse. You can choose something you'll never be thanked for. Just choose something you can keep. One seva, kept, does more than ten, dropped.
screen: `SEVA IS A RHYTHM.` · `THE GURDWARA RUNS ON MORNINGS.` · `SMALL ACTS BORE THE EGO.` · `SMALL, SPECIFIC, REGULAR.` · then, large: `ONE SEVA, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the week's sevas pass in front of you. The unseen kindness. The shoes. The dish. The tenth. The thing you taught. Which one felt most like you? Now make it small enough to keep every week. Give it a day, and a time. Picture yourself doing it next week, and the week after, and in six months, when nobody remembers you started. If you pray, you can offer it. The bell holds the time.
Your weekly seva. One small, regular service, chosen to be kept, which does its quiet work over months and years.
Your line: one seva, kept. Today, write your weekly seva somewhere you'll see it, with its day. Tomorrow, kirtan begins. Day one hundred three.

104.title: Just listening
104.hook: kirtan is the singing of the Guru's hymns, and the first practice is simply to listen
104.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, musicians called ragis sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib while the congregation listens, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar kirtan continues for most of the day and is broadcast live.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your weekly seva, chosen small enough to keep. Your line was one seva, kept. Did you write it down, with its day? Day one hundred four.

There's probably a song you've heard a hundred times and never actually listened to. It plays in the store, in the car, in the background of your life. Then one day you hear it with headphones, eyes closed, and you catch the harmony underneath, a line you never noticed. It's like a different song. Now go to the Golden Temple in Amritsar, before dawn. From the center of the pool, music is already drifting out across the water. Voices, a harmonium, a drum. It goes on almost all day, every day. People sit along the walkway with their eyes closed. They're not singing. They're not reading. They're just listening.
screen: `THE SONG YOU NEVER HEARD.` → `AMRITSAR, BEFORE DAWN.` → `EYES CLOSED, JUST LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, the shabads of the Guru Granth Sahib, set to music. It's at the heart of Sikh worship. Think back to the very beginning of the stories, on day thirty-one: Guru Nanak didn't write his hymns to be read silently. He sang them, with Mardana playing the rebab beside him. The Gurus were musicians. Most of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by musical mood, which is tomorrow's word. So for Sikhs, the Word comes most fully alive when it's sung. Guru Arjan says it plainly. In paraphrase: in this dark age, kirtan, singing the praises of God, is the highest practice. And there's a practical reason too. Music gets past the part of you that argues. You can resist an idea. It's harder to resist a melody. Now here's where camp three starts: not with singing, but with listening. The Japji, you'll remember, gives four whole stanzas to listening. Kirtan begins the same way. Before you learn a tune or a word, you let the sound in. You don't have to understand Gurmukhi. You don't have to know what raga it's in. You don't have to feel anything special. Just listen, the way you'd listen to a friend telling you something important. Sikhs say the sound itself does something, that listening to gurbani with attention is already a kind of remembering. Over the coming days, you'll move from listening to singing. Today, it's only your ears.
screen: `KIRTAN — SINGING THE HYMNS.` · `THE GURUS WERE MUSICIANS.` · `IN THIS AGE, KIRTAN IS HIGHEST.` · `FIRST, ONLY YOUR EARS.` · then, large: `JUST LISTEN.`

segments.voice: If you can, find a recording of one shabad, any one, and play it now. Many gurdwaras stream their kirtan live, including the Golden Temple. If you can't, simply listen to the room around you. Close your eyes. Don't try to understand. Don't hum along yet. Let the sound arrive, the voice, the drum, the pause between phrases. When your mind drifts away, come back to the sound, as many times as it takes. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, and for camp three, the practice that begins with simply listening.
Your line: just listen. Today, listen to one shabad all the way through, doing nothing else. No phone, no dishes. Just ears. Day one hundred four.

screen: `DAY 104 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOOD OF A RAGA.`

105.title: The mood of a raga
105.hook: each hymn of the Granth is set in a raga, a musical mood for the words
105.howItsDone: Each shabad in the Guru Granth Sahib is headed with its raag, and trained kirtan musicians sing it in that raag; some gurdwaras and schools work to keep the traditional raag settings alive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan, the Guru's hymns sung, and the first practice of it. Your line was just listen. Did you hear one shabad all the way through? Day one hundred five.

Movie composers know something the rest of us feel without naming. Before a single word is spoken, the music tells you what kind of scene this is. A few low notes, and you know something's wrong. A bright little tune, and you know it's morning and everyone's fine. Take the same line of dialogue, play different music under it, and it means something else. Now imagine a book of scripture where every single hymn comes with that instruction built in. Not just the words, but the mood they should be sung in. That's how the Guru Granth Sahib is organized, and it's today's word.
screen: `THE MUSIC TELLS YOU THE SCENE.` → `SAME WORDS, DIFFERENT MEANING.` → `A SCRIPTURE WITH MOODS BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: Raag. In English you'll often see it spelled raga. It's a musical framework from Indian classical music: a set of notes, a shape of melody, and above all a mood. The Guru Granth Sahib is divided by raag. After the opening prayers, the hymns are grouped into sections, thirty-one main raags, and every hymn carries its raag in its heading. Open to almost any page and the first thing written above a shabad is its musical mood. Each raag has a feeling, and many have a time of day or a season. Basant is spring, bright and fresh. Malhar is the monsoon, when rain breaks a long heat. Some are for dawn, some for evening, some carry longing, some peace. The Gurus chose them on purpose, so the music would carry the meaning of the words, not fight it. The first raag in the Granth is Sri Raag. Guru Amar Das says of it, in paraphrase, that among the raags Sri Raag is the best, but only if through it you come to love the True One. That line tells you how the Gurus saw music. The raag serves the Word. Music isn't the point; it's the vehicle. And when kirtan is sung in its raag, the listener feels the mood before understanding a single word. Look back at this week and you'll see the same shape. Seva of the hands, the purse and the mind, haumai, your weekly seva, kirtan, and now raag: the teaching carried into the body, the wallet, the voice and the ear.
screen: `RAAG — A MUSICAL MOOD.` · `THIRTY-ONE RAAGS, EACH IN ITS HEADING.` · `SPRING, MONSOON, DAWN, EVENING.` · `THE RAAG SERVES THE WORD.` · then, large: `MUSIC CARRIES MEANING.`

segments.voice: Play one song or one shabad, anything with music. Or remember one you know well. Close your eyes. Before you think about the words, ask: what's the mood here? Morning or night? Longing or peace? Heavy or light? Don't name it too fast. Let the feeling show up in your body first: in your chest, your shoulders, your breath. Then notice how the mood shapes the words, if there are any. The bell holds the time.
Raag. A musical mood, and the way the Guru Granth Sahib is ordered, so each hymn is sung in a feeling that fits its words. Your week: hands, purse, mind, haumai, your weekly seva, kirtan, and raag.
Your line: music carries meaning. Today, notice the mood of one song before you notice its words. Day one hundred five.
